Philippians
fih-LIP-ee-unz
noun (proper)
From Greek Philippēsioi (Φιλιππήσιοι) — the inhabitants of Philippi, a Roman colony in Macedonia named for Philip II of Macedon; title of Paul's most affectionate prison letter, addressed to his first European congregation and containing the great kenosis hymn and the apostle's own testimony of justification.

See also: Philippians

Biblical Definition

The Epistle to the Philippians is one of Paul's prison letters, written from Rome circa AD 61–62 to the first church planted on European soil (Acts 16:12–40), a congregation with whom Paul maintained a unique partnership in the gospel (Phil 1:5). The letter's dominant tone is joy — the word or its cognates appear sixteen times in four chapters — all the more remarkable because Paul writes from chains with his life uncertain. The theological crown is the carmen Christi (Phil 2:5–11): the pre-existent Son of God “But made himself of no reputation, and took upon him the form of a servant, and was made in the likeness of men:” (Phil 2:7). This self-humiliation was not a subtraction of divine nature but the veiling of divine prerogatives in willing condescension to human form and the death of the cross — followed by God's exaltation of Him to the name above every name. Chapter 3 is the biographical centerpiece: Paul counts all former credentials as rubbish for the surpassing worth of knowing Christ Jesus as Lord and being found in Him, “And be found in him, not having mine own righteousness, which is of the law, but that which is through the faith of Christ, the righteousness which is of God by faith:” (Phil 3:9). The letter closes with the most famous contentment text in Scripture: “Not that I speak in respect of want: for I have learned, in whatsoever state I am, therewith to be content.” (Phil 4:11) — learned through suffering, not inherited from temperament, and possible only through Christ who strengthens (Phil 4:13).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster does not record “Philippians” as a common English noun; it names the inhabitants of the Macedonian Roman colony of Philippi and the Pauline prison epistle addressed to their church — remarkable for its joy, its kenosis Christology, its polemic against works-righteousness, and its doctrine of contentment.

PHILIPPIANS, n. pl. [From Philippi, a Roman colony in Macedonia.] The residents of Philippi; specifically, the recipients of Paul's prison epistle — a letter remarkable for its pastoral warmth, its Christ-hymn (the kenosis passage), its polemic against Jewish works-righteousness, and its meditation on joy, contentment, and the peace that surpasses all understanding.

Reformed commentators from Calvin to Moule and Moo have read Philippians as the apostle's most personal disclosure of what justification by faith alone looks like when internalized into the affections: all boasting in the flesh stripped away, Christ gained, righteousness received by faith, suffering embraced, and contentment achieved not through circumstances but through Him who strengthens.

The carmen Christi (Phil 2:5–11) provides the Incarnation's narrative in miniature: pre-existent divine equality, voluntary condescension to human form and death, and God's sovereign exaltation to universal lordship — the movement that governs all Christian ethics and all Christian hope.

Key Scripture

Phil 1:21 — "For to me, to live is Christ — and to die is gain."

Phil 2:7 — "But made himself of no reputation, and took upon him the form of a servant, and was made in the likeness of men:"

Phil 3:9 — "And be found in him, not having mine own righteousness, which is of the law, but that which is through the faith of Christ, the righteousness which is of God by faith:"

Phil 4:11 — "Not that I speak in respect of want: for I have learned, in whatsoever state I am, therewith to be content."

Modern Corruption

Nineteenth-century kenotic Christology exploited Phil 2:5–11 to deny the Son's full divinity during the Incarnation; the contentment texts have been sentimentalized into therapeutic positivity divorced from their suffering and christological context.

expand to see more

The carmen Christi (Phil 2:5–11) was badly mishandled by nineteenth-century “kenotic Christology” (Gottfried Thomasius, Charles Gore), which interpreted “emptied Himself” (ekenōsen) as a literal subtraction of divine attributes — omniscience, omnipotence, omnipresence — during the Incarnation, leaving the incarnate Christ with limited divine capacities. This directly contradicts Chalcedonian orthodoxy: the divine nature is immutable and impassible; the Son did not surrender any divine attribute. The emptying is the willing assumption of a second nature and the veiling of divine glory in the servant form, not a diminution of divine being. Modern kenotic Christology continues in various forms under the banner of “social trinitarianism,” often making the Incarnation a permanent ontological change in the Son — a departure from classical theism the Reformed tradition rightly resists.

The contentment texts (Phil 4:6–7, 11–13) have been absorbed into therapeutic self-help culture as generalizable techniques for mental wellness. The “mindfulness” reading strips them of their theological content (Paul's contentment comes through Christ who strengthens, not through cognitive reframing) and their suffering context (Paul writes from a Roman prison, not a retreat center). Progressive readings further spiritualize Phil 3:8's “all things as loss” into invitations for social privilege-surrender rather than the apostle's categorical renunciation of all self-achieved righteousness before God.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Rooted in the Greek name of the Macedonian city Philippi and the key Pauline terms kenōsis (“emptying”) and autarkes (“content”) — the letter's two most theologically charged and most abused terms.

expand to see more

Philippi — a Roman colony in Macedonia, named for Philip II; site of the battle of 42 BC; Paul's first European congregation, planted through the conversion of Lydia and the Philippian jailer (Acts 16)

Greek ekenōsen (ἐκένωσεν) — he emptied himself; the verbal root of “kenosis”; denotes the Son's voluntary self-humiliation in assuming humanity, not a surrender of divine nature but a veiling of divine prerogatives

Greek autarkes (αὐτάρκης) — self-sufficient, content; a Stoic philosophical term Paul baptizes into a Christ-dependent virtue — contentment learned through affliction and possible only through Christ's enabling (Phil 4:13)

Greek hyperyphōsen (ὑπερύψωσεν) — highly exalted; God's response to the Son's humiliation in Phil 2:9 — the exaltation is commensurate with the condescension, culminating in universal lordship and every knee bowing

Latin gaudium — joy; the theological fruit of justification and union with Christ — the soil in which Philippians' repeated “rejoice in the Lord” (Phil 4:4) grows, independent of outward circumstance because rooted in the risen Christ

Usage

"The carmen Christi (Phil 2:5–11) is the New Testament's defining narrative of the Incarnation as voluntary self-humiliation: the Son who was in the form of God took the form of a servant — not losing divinity but veiling its prerogatives in the obedience of a bondservant unto death."

"Philippians 3:8–9 is Paul's autobiography of justification: every advantage of birth, zeal, and legal observance counted as rubbish that he might be found in Christ with a righteousness not his own — the forensic grammar of the gospel in personal testimony form."

"Paul's contentment (Phil 4:11) is not Stoic resignation but a christological virtue: “I can do all things through Him who strengthens me” (4:13) — it is learned through suffering and exercised by grace, making it simultaneously the most demanding and the most liberating word in the epistle."
